brief.situation: 20:00 on an orthopedic unit. You are the RN for Mrs. Abara, 88, on day 1 after surgical repair of a hip fracture. She has advanced dementia and speaks only a few words. Her daughter is at the bedside.
handover: The care plan says: pain assessed with the 0-10 numeric scale every 4 hours; the ordered oral analgesic as needed 'when the patient requests'. Every score today is charted '0 - denies pain' and she has had no analgesic since surgery.
Since 18:00 she has been moaning, grabbing at the rails and pushing staff away when turned. The evening nurse suggested the as-needed antipsychotic 'for agitation'.

Unit policy: for a patient who cannot self-report, the nurse uses a validated observational pain tool, may give an ordered as-needed analgesic on its findings, and calls the provider to change a plan that is not working.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Untreated pain drives agitation and delirium. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
It settles once her pain is treated and the plan is changed. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

why.question: Why is Mrs. Abara's plan failing, and what do you change?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: The plan relies on self-report and requests she cannot make, so '0' scores and 'pain controlled' are false; her behavior and a PAINAD of 8 show severe pain after hip surgery.
parts.modelAnswer: The plan only works if she can tell us or ask, and she can't. So the zeros are wrong, and the moaning and pushing away are pain. Her PAINAD is 8.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Uses PAINAD, gives the ordered as-needed analgesic and nondrug comfort, avoids antipsychotics and restraint, asks her daughter how she shows pain, and calls the provider to change to scheduled analgesia with PAINAD-based reassessment.
parts.modelAnswer: Score her with PAINAD, give the as-needed analgesic and her blanket and music, no antipsychotic or restraints, ask her daughter what her pain looks like, and call to get scheduled pain medicine and a PAINAD plan.

noProgress.rationale: Severe untreated pain an hour on is harm here.

delirium.headline: Delirium and a fall
delirium.body: A person who cannot self-report will chart '0' on a numeric scale. Use an observational tool, treat the pain, and change the plan; sedation and restraint make delirium and falls more likely.

safe.headline: Plan changed to fit her
safe.body: You saw the plan's outcome was false, used an observational tool, treated pain rather than 'agitation', involved her daughter and called to change the plan within minutes. That is the expert path.

safeGaps.headline: Changed, with gaps
safeGaps.body: Check how soon you called, whether she was sedated or restrained, and whether you scored her with an observational tool.

time_up.headline: Unchanged at 21:00
time_up.body: A plan whose outcomes are false must change now.

scoring.modelReasoning: Evaluation decides whether a plan continues, changes or ends. Mrs. Abara's plan assumed self-report and requests she cannot make, so its outcome ('pain controlled') was false. For a person with advanced dementia, use an observational tool such as PAINAD (breathing, vocalization, facial expression, body language, consolability; 0-10), treat pain with the ordered analgesic and her own comforts, and rescore after the intervention. Antipsychotics and restraint for 'agitation' that is really pain raise the risk of delirium and falls. Call the provider to change the plan to scheduled analgesia and PAINAD-based reassessment, built with her daughter.
